metaData.title: After Automation
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: The more we automate with AI, the more expert human work is created, as commoditized output demands human judgment for differentiation and quality.
metaData.summary: Dan Shipper, CEO of Every, argues that AI automation paradoxically increases the demand for expert human work, rather than eliminating it. Drawing on internal experience at Every, he describes two modes of working with agents: agent employees (coworker and embedded) and human-AI collaboration in tools like Codex and Claude Code. He explains that AI commoditizes the residue of past human competence, making it cheap and abundant. This abundance creates sameness (slop), which in turn creates demand for differentiated, high-status work that only humans can provide. He addresses the objection of exponential benchmark progress by arguing that benchmarks measure performance inside a fixed frame, and saturating one frame simply creates new demand for experts who can adapt that competence to novel, live problems. The essay concludes that the future of knowledge work is not replacement, but a continuous cycle of automation creating new, higher-value human roles.
metaData.featuredReason: This piece delves into the paradox of AI automation, asserting that making competence cheap paradoxically creates more demand for human experts. It explains how humans continuously shift the “frame” of valuable work, staying ahead of AI's benchmark-driven progress. The author argues that true “agency”—the ability to want for oneself—remains a uniquely human trait, distinguishing us from even the most advanced AI agents.

mainPoints.point: AI automation creates more expert human work, not less.
mainPoints.explanation: At Every, despite automating heavily, the team has grown and human work has increased. Agents require human oversight, maintenance, and judgment to function effectively.

mainPoints.point: AI commoditizes the visible residue of past human competence, making it cheap and abundant.
mainPoints.explanation: Models are trained on completed work (code, prose, etc.), making these skills broadly available. This abundance leads to sameness (slop) in output.

mainPoints.point: Sameness creates a demand for difference, which only humans can provide.
mainPoints.explanation: When AI output is generic and indistinguishable, humans seek work that feels alive, specific, and high-status. This demand for differentiation is new demand for human experts.

mainPoints.point: Benchmark progress is real but occurs inside a fixed frame; saturating one frame creates new demand for experts.
mainPoints.explanation: Benchmarks measure performance on a specific prompt and task. Once a frame is saturated, the work inside it becomes cheap, leading to more attempts and a greater need for expert judgment to adapt and validate.

keyQuotes: There is a paradox at the heart of AI. ... the more we automate, the more expert human work there is to do.
AI commoditizes the residue of human expertise—whatever can be made explicit enough to train on. That collapses the value of default model output and creates demand for what's different.
When work is abundant and looks alike everywhere, the work that doesn't fit the pattern becomes the rare, valuable, and high-status thing.
The current generation of models only knows about work that has been done. Humans know about what needs to be done, right now, at this moment.
Making expert work cheaper does not simply replace experts. It creates more situations where expert judgment is needed.

relatedArticles.title: Why Anthropic Thinks AI Should Have Its Own Computer — Felix Rieseberg of Claude Cowork & Claude Code Desktop
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Felix Rieseberg discusses why Anthropic believes the future of AI lies in trusted task execution through local-first agent workflows, where AI has its own computer to work with rather than just chat interfaces.

relatedArticles.title: I Let ChatGPT Manage My Workweek
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: A writer builds a ChatGPT agent to manage her project management weaknesses, using OKRs, Notion, calendar, and Slack integrations to automate weekly planning and status reporting.

relatedArticles.title: AI Work Is Splitting in Two
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This newsletter edition reports on the bifurcation of AI work into two distinct modes: delegation to long-running agents and real-time collaboration with desktop tools, highlighted by Anthropic's Code with Claude developer conference and the launch of new Managed Agents features.

relatedArticles.title: Introducing routines in Claude Code
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Claude Code introduces 'routines', a new feature allowing developers to configure automated workflows (prompt + repo + connectors) that run on a schedule, via API calls, or in response to events like GitHub webhooks.

relatedArticles.title: New Future of Work 2025: AI is Driving Rapid Change, but Uneven Benefits
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: The Microsoft New Future of Work 2025 report highlights that generative AI is shifting from a mere productivity tool to an active collaborative partner, while warning of uneven adoption, the risk of 'workslop', and the increasing necessity of human judgment and expertise.

relatedArticles.title: OpenClaw v2026.3.7 Release: GPT-5.4 Support and Infrastructure Upgrades
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenClaw releases version 2026.3.7, featuring support for GPT-5.4 and Gemini 3.1, along with significant infrastructure and connectivity improvements.

relatedArticles.title: What I Learned Onboarding Our AI Project Manager
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article details the practical lessons learned from building and onboarding an AI project manager agent, emphasizing the need for clear job definition, understanding context window limitations, creating a detailed handbook, and iterative management.

relatedArticles.title: The Culture of AI Engineering
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article argues that the 'software factory' metaphor is wrong for AI engineering, proposing instead a cultural framework inspired by Stewart Brand's pace layers to align humans and AI agents toward a shared creative vision.

relatedArticles.title: Codex for Everyday Work: AI Agents Beyond Coding
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI's Head of Codex Tibo Sio explains how Codex has evolved from a developer tool into a general-purpose agent that automates knowledge work, demos personal software creation, and previews the long-horizon Slash Goal mode and Auto Review safety agent.

relatedArticles.title: Claude Code for Product Managers
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: A product manager shares how Claude Code eliminates PM drudgery by handling roadmap breakdown, ticket creation, and user analytics, freeing him to focus on strategy and creative thinking.
